# MOVING DAY ESSENTIALS — Keep in the Car

*Print this page. Tape it to a clipboard or keep it in the glovebox.*

---

**DOCUMENTS (one folder or pouch)**
- [ ] Driver's licenses and passports
- [ ] Vehicle title, registration, insurance card
- [ ] Lease or closing papers (both homes)
- [ ] Moving contract, Bill of Lading, inventory sheet
- [ ] Vehicle shipping receipt and carrier contact info
- [ ] Dog: rabies cert, vaccine records, microchip number, vet phone
- [ ] Copies of prescriptions (all household members)
- [ ] Insurance policy numbers (auto, renters/home, health)
- [ ] Emergency contacts list (printed, not just on your phone)

**PERSONAL BAGS (one per person, packed like a 3-night trip)**
- [ ] 3 changes of clothes, pajamas, underwear, socks
- [ ] Toiletries, medications, glasses/contacts
- [ ] Phone chargers, laptop, earbuds
- [ ] Wallet, keys (old home, new home, car spare)
- [ ] Snacks and refillable water bottles

**DOG KIT (one bag or bin)**
- [ ] Food (enough for 4–5 days), treats, collapsible bowls
- [ ] Leash, harness, collar with current ID tag
- [ ] Poop bags, paper towels, pet-safe cleaner
- [ ] Crate or car barrier/seatbelt harness
- [ ] Familiar blanket or bed, one favorite toy
- [ ] Any medications or calming aids
- [ ] Vet records folder (duplicate of what's in the doc pouch)
- [ ] Recent photo of the dog on your phone (in case of separation)

**CAR EMERGENCY KIT**
- [ ] Jumper cables or portable jump starter
- [ ] Tire pressure gauge, spare tire confirmed inflated
- [ ] First aid kit
- [ ] Flashlight and batteries
- [ ] Roadside assistance number saved and printed
- [ ] Paper maps or downloaded offline maps (I-80 and I-84 have dead zones)
- [ ] Blanket, rain jacket

**CLEANING AND LOCKUP (before you leave the old place)**
- [ ] Final walkthrough — open every closet, cabinet, drawer
- [ ] Photograph every room, the exterior, and the meter readings
- [ ] Return keys, garage remotes, fobs — get a written receipt
- [ ] Confirm trash is out, thermostat is set, and windows/doors are locked
- [ ] Text or call landlord to confirm move-out is complete

**ARRIVAL (first things at the new place)**
- [ ] Photograph every room before unloading — document existing damage
- [ ] Locate breaker box, water shutoff, gas shutoff
- [ ] Confirm utilities are live (lights, water, heat/AC)
- [ ] Unload the dog kit first — set up a safe, quiet space with water and a familiar blanket
- [ ] Unload personal bags — set up beds or air mattresses before the truck arrives
- [ ] Check phone signal and Wi-Fi

---
---

# 8-WEEK MOVE COUNTDOWN — Phone Calendar Reminders

*Copy each line into your calendar app as an all-day event or reminder. Adjust dates to your actual move day.*

---

**WEEK 8 (56 days out)**
- [ ] Give written notice to landlord. Photograph the notice and save it.
- [ ] Get 3–4 moving quotes (or reserve DIY truck/container).
- [ ] Start Oregon housing search if not already signed.
- [ ] Book vet visit for dog — get records, rabies cert, and health check.
- [ ] Check vehicle title location — you'll need it for Oregon registration.

**WEEK 7 (49 days out)**
- [ ] Choose mover or DIY option and book the date. Pay deposit.
- [ ] Get 2–3 vehicle shipping quotes (if shipping a car).
- [ ] Plan driving route — book dog-friendly hotels for 2–3 overnight stops.
- [ ] Schedule internet installation at Oregon address (long lead times).
- [ ] Start declutter: garage, storage, and closets this week.

**WEEK 6 (42 days out)**
- [ ] Confirm Oregon lease signed or closing date locked.
- [ ] Book temporary housing if the new place won't be ready on arrival.
- [ ] Order packing supplies (boxes, tape, bubble wrap, markers).
- [ ] Begin packing: storage rooms, guest room, out-of-season clothes.
- [ ] Gather all important documents into one folder (see documents list).

**WEEK 5 (35 days out)**
- [ ] File USPS change of address (usps.com). Set the start date ~2 days before move.
- [ ] Notify banks, credit cards, and insurance companies of upcoming address change.
- [ ] Schedule Ohio utility shutoffs for the day after you leave.
- [ ] Schedule Oregon utility startups for the day before you arrive.
- [ ] Continue packing: bookshelves, decor, dining room, rarely used kitchen items.

**WEEK 4 (28 days out)**
- [ ] Confirm mover or truck reservation — get the final written estimate.
- [ ] Confirm vehicle shipping pickup date (if applicable).
- [ ] Sell or donate items you're not moving — schedule charity pickups.
- [ ] Update employer payroll with new address. Confirm remote work or start date.
- [ ] Continue packing: remaining living areas, office, kids' rooms (if any).

**WEEK 3 (21 days out)**
- [ ] Call auto insurance — confirm coverage for Oregon and the drive.
- [ ] Get a dog ID tag with your new phone number or destination address.
- [ ] Pack: bathrooms (leave one set of toiletries), linens, most of the kitchen.
- [ ] Cancel or transfer subscriptions and memberships (gym, CSA, newspaper, etc.).
- [ ] Arrange pet sitter or boarding for moving day if needed.

**WEEK 2 (14 days out)**
- [ ] Confirm all hotel reservations along the route.
- [ ] Confirm internet install date in Oregon.
- [ ] Finish packing all rooms except daily-use items.
- [ ] Prep the "moving day essentials" car kit (see one-pager).
- [ ] Photograph valuables and serial numbers — save to phone and a USB drive.

**WEEK 1 (7 days out)**
- [ ] Defrost and clean fridge/freezer. Donate perishable food.
- [ ] Do a final car check: oil, tires, fluids, battery, wipers.
- [ ] Confirm mover arrival time and payment method.
- [ ] Pack the dog travel kit — food, bowls, leash, meds, blanket, toy, records.
- [ ] Download offline maps for your route (I-80 and I-84 corridors).

**DAY BEFORE**
- [ ] Final loads into boxes. Tape and label everything.
- [ ] Charge all devices overnight.
- [ ] Set out clothes and toiletries for tomorrow.
- [ ] Load car kit, dog kit, and personal bags into the car tonight.
- [ ] Get sleep. Tomorrow is a long day.

**MOVE DAY**
- [ ] Walk through every room, closet, cabinet, and drawer.
- [ ] Photograph every room and meter readings.
- [ ] Supervise loading — check the inventory and Bill of Lading before signing.
- [ ] Return keys, get receipt, text landlord.
- [ ] Hit the road. First stop in 2–3 hours for the dog.

**WEEK +1 (after arrival)**
- [ ] Photograph the new place before unpacking — document any existing damage.
- [ ] Get Oregon driver's license and register vehicle (check the deadline).
- [ ] Schedule emissions test if in Portland metro or other required areas.
- [ ] First Oregon vet visit — transfer records, get dog license.
- [ ] Update microchip registry, voter registration, and remaining accounts.

---

Both of these are plain text so you can paste them straight into a notes app, Google Doc, or word processor. For the calendar reminders, the easiest approach is to create a shared Google or Apple calendar called "Move Countdown," then add each week's items as individual all-day events on the right dates. That way you both get notifications and can check things off from your phones.

# ROOM-BY-ROOM PACKING CHECKLIST

**Labeling scheme:** Every box gets three things written on two sides and the top in thick marker: (1) the room name, (2) a short contents description, and (3) a priority tag. Use three priority tags: **OPEN FIRST** for things you need the first night, **SOON** for the first week, and **LATER** for everything else. Example: *"KITCHEN — coffee maker, mugs, filters — OPEN FIRST."* Number boxes sequentially within each room (Kitchen 1 of 8, Kitchen 2 of 8, etc.) so you can spot a missing box immediately.

---

## KITCHEN

**Estimated time:** 6–10 hours across two sessions (pack rarely used items first, daily items last)
**Estimated boxes:** 8–15 (kitchens are deceptively box-heavy because of fragile items)

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Specialty appliances you rarely use (bread maker, food processor, waffle iron)
- [ ] Bakeware, roasting pans, holiday dishes
- [ ] Cookbooks, decorative items, vases
- [ ] Extra utensils, duplicate tools, gadgets you forgot you had
- [ ] Entertaining supplies (platters, punch bowls, candles, table linens)

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Most pots, pans, and mixing bowls (keep one pot, one pan, one spatula out)
- [ ] Plates, glasses, mugs (wrap each individually in packing paper — never newspaper, the ink transfers)
- [ ] Knives in blade guards or wrapped in towels and taped
- [ ] Small appliances (toaster, blender)
- [ ] Pantry dry goods that are sealed and worth moving (spices, oils, canned goods)

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] The one pot, one pan, one spatula you kept out
- [ ] Coffee maker, last two mugs, dish soap, sponge, hand towel
- [ ] Trash bags, paper towels, cleaning spray (keep these accessible until the very end)

**Declutter tips:** Toss or donate anything chipped, warped, missing lids, or duplicated. Spices older than a year have lost most of their flavor. Half-empty condiments and open pantry items aren't worth moving 2,400 miles. If you haven't used a gadget in a year, donate it.

---

## LIVING ROOM

**Estimated time:** 3–5 hours
**Estimated boxes:** 5–10

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Books, DVDs, games, board games (use small boxes — book boxes get brutally heavy)
- [ ] Decorative items, picture frames, wall art (wrap frames in bubble wrap or towels; label FRAGILE)
- [ ] Throw pillows, blankets you don't use daily
- [ ] Candles, coasters, shelf decor, plants you're not bringing

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Electronics: TV, gaming console, speakers, streaming devices. Photograph cable setups before unplugging. Coil cords and label them or put each device's cables in a labeled zip-lock bag taped to the device.
- [ ] Lamps (remove bulbs, wrap shades separately — they crush easily)
- [ ] Remaining blankets and throw pillows
- [ ] Curtains and rods if you're taking them

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] The one blanket and pillow you used last night
- [ ] Remote controls, charging cables you used overnight
- [ ] Any cleaning supplies you used for the final wipe-down

**Declutter tips:** Books are the single heaviest category per cubic foot. Be ruthless. If you won't re-read it and it's not sentimental, donate it. Old cables, remotes for devices you no longer own, and dead batteries can go.

---

## BEDROOM(S)

**Estimated time:** 3–5 hours per bedroom
**Estimated boxes:** 5–8 per bedroom

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Off-season clothing, formal wear, costumes
- [ ] Extra bedding sets, decorative pillows, spare blankets
- [ ] Jewelry you don't wear daily (carry valuable jewelry with you, not in the truck)
- [ ] Nightstand clutter: old magazines, books you've finished, random chargers
- [ ] Under-bed storage items

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Most clothing. Wardrobe boxes (tall, with a hanging rod) are worth the extra cost for nice clothes. For everything else, leave clothes in dresser drawers and wrap the dresser in moving blankets; the weight is usually fine.
- [ ] Shoes (stuff socks inside to save space and hold shape)
- [ ] Remaining bedding except what you'll sleep on the last night
- [ ] Mirrors and artwork (wrap in bubble wrap, stand upright, label FRAGILE and THIS SIDE UP)

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] The sheets, pillows, and blanket you slept on. Roll them into a trash bag and toss them in the car for the first night at the new place.
- [ ] Phone charger, alarm clock, bedside lamp
- [ ] Air mattress or sleeping bag if you used one the last night

**Declutter tips:** Try everything on. If it doesn't fit, isn't flattering, or hasn't been worn in a year, donate it. Shoes with worn soles aren't worth the box space. Old pillows that have lost their loft should be replaced, not moved.

---

## BATHROOM(S)

**Estimated time:** 1–2 hours per bathroom
**Estimated boxes:** 2–4 per bathroom

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Guest bathroom entirely (if you have one)
- [ ] Backup toiletries, bulk supplies, extra towels
- [ ] Medicine cabinet: expired medications (dispose safely at a pharmacy drop-off), first aid supplies, rarely used items
- [ ] Hair tools you don't use daily
- [ ] Cleaning supplies under the sink (seal lids with tape and bag them upright in a plastic bin)

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Most towels (keep two per person)
- [ ] Most toiletries (keep daily essentials in a zip-lock bag)
- [ ] Shower curtain, bath mat, wastebasket

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] Toothbrushes, toothpaste, deodorant, face wash, contacts solution — straight into your personal bag
- [ ] Last two towels — damp is fine, stuff them in a plastic bag
- [ ] Toilet paper (keep one roll accessible until the very end, and put a fresh roll in the car for the new place)

**Declutter tips:** Expired medications and sunscreen go. Mostly-empty bottles, old razors, travel-sized products from hotels, and stained towels can all be tossed. If you have seven half-used shampoo bottles, consolidate into one.

---

## HOME OFFICE

**Estimated time:** 3–5 hours
**Estimated boxes:** 4–8

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Books, reference materials, old notebooks
- [ ] Supplies you rarely use (extra printer ink, envelopes, old stationery)
- [ ] Filing cabinet contents: shred anything older than 7 years for taxes, or anything you don't need. Keep the last 3 years of tax returns, contracts, and legal documents.
- [ ] Spare cables, old hard drives, peripherals you don't use

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Printer (remove ink cartridges, bag them separately)
- [ ] Monitor (original box is best; otherwise wrap in a moving blanket and stand upright)
- [ ] Desk accessories, desk lamp, bulletin board contents
- [ ] Photograph your desk and cable setup before dismantling

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] Laptop, charger, mouse — these go in your personal bag, not a box
- [ ] Any external drives or USB sticks with important data — carry these with you
- [ ] Desk phone or headset if you're working remotely during the transition

**Declutter tips:** Old manuals for products you no longer own, dead pens, dried-out markers, and broken office chairs aren't worth moving. Scan important papers and save them to cloud storage before shredding the originals if you're comfortable with digital-only copies.

---

## GARAGE / STORAGE / UTILITY AREAS

**Estimated time:** 4–8 hours (this is usually the worst room because it's been ignored the longest)
**Estimated boxes / bins:** 5–15 depending on how much you've accumulated

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out — start here if you can)**
- [ ] Seasonal items (holiday decorations, camping gear, sports equipment)
- [ ] Tools: keep a basic toolkit out (screwdriver, pliers, hammer, tape measure, box cutter) for disassembling furniture. Pack the rest.
- [ ] Lawn and garden tools — decide what's worth moving vs. selling or donating
- [ ] Paint cans, solvents, propane, aerosols — these cannot go on a moving truck. Use them up, give them away, or dispose of them through your local hazardous waste program.
- [ ] Bikes, strollers, large toys

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Remaining tools except the basic toolkit
- [ ] Cleaning supplies you're bringing (seal and bag them)
- [ ] Extension cords, flashlights, batteries

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] Basic toolkit (last thing in, first thing out — you'll need it to reassemble furniture)
- [ ] Broom and dustpan for the final sweep
- [ ] Remaining cleaning supplies

**Declutter tips:** This room has the highest percentage of things that aren't worth moving. Broken items, rusty tools, dried-out paint, mystery hardware, and furniture you've been meaning to fix for two years can go. If you wouldn't buy it again, don't pay to move it.

---

## CLOSETS (hall, coat, linen, entry)

**Estimated time:** 1–3 hours total
**Estimated boxes:** 2–5

**Pack early (2–3 weeks out)**
- [ ] Linen closet: extra sheet sets, tablecloths, towels beyond what you've kept out
- [ ] Coat closet: off-season jackets, scarves, hats, gloves, umbrellas
- [ ] Hall closet: board games, crafts, luggage (use luggage as packing containers for soft items)
- [ ] Entry closet: shoes, bags, reusable shopping bags

**Pack last week**
- [ ] Remaining coats and jackets
- [ ] Vacuum cleaner (but keep it accessible for the final clean)
- [ ] Ironing board, iron, hangers you're keeping

**Pack moving day morning**
- [ ] Vacuum cleaner after the final pass
- [ ] Last coats or jackets

**Declutter tips:** Wire hangers can go back to the dry cleaner. Mismatched sheet sets, threadbare towels, and broken umbrellas aren't worth packing. If you have more luggage than you use on your most ambitious trip, donate the extras.

---

## BOX COUNT SUMMARY (1–2 bedroom apartment, two adults)

| Room | Estimated Boxes |
|---|---|
| Kitchen | 8–15 |
| Living Room | 5–10 |
| Bedroom 1 (primary) | 5–8 |
| Bedroom 2 (guest/spare) | 3–6 |
| Bathroom(s) | 2–4 each |
| Home Office | 4–8 |
| Garage / Storage | 5–15 |
| Closets (all) | 2–5 |
| **Total estimate** | **34–71** |

Order 10–15% more boxes than you think you'll need. You'll use them. Small boxes for heavy things (books, tools, cans), medium for general items, large for light bulky things (pillows, lampshades, linens). Never put heavy items in large boxes.

---
---

# SERVICES & SUBSCRIPTIONS: CANCELLATION AND START TIMELINE

**General rule:** Cancel Ohio services for the day *after* you leave (so you have service on your last full day). Start Oregon services for the day *before* you arrive (so they're live when you walk in). Confirm everything in writing or by email, and screenshot the confirmations.

---

## UTILITIES

| Service | Who | When to Cancel (Ohio) | When to Start (Oregon) | Lead Time Needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Electricity | **M** | 5–7 business days before move-out. Schedule final read. | 5–7 business days before arrival. May need a deposit or SSN. | 1 week |
| Gas / heating | **M** | Same as electric. Often the same provider in Ohio. | Same as electric. | 1 week |
| Water / sewer / trash | **P** | Some cities require 3–5 days' notice. Check if these are bundled through the city. | Often auto-starts with the landlord or city; confirm with your new city or landlord. | 1 week |
| Internet / cable | **P** | 1–2 weeks' notice. Return equipment to avoid fees. Get a return receipt. | 2–4 weeks' notice — installation appointments book out. Schedule ASAP. | 2–4 weeks |
| Streaming (Netflix, Hulu, etc.) | **J** | No cancellation needed unless you want to pause. Update billing address and payment method. | Same accounts, just update address. | Day of |

## INSURANCE

| Service | Who | When to Notify | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Auto insurance | **M** | 2–3 weeks before move. Call your carrier. | You may need to switch to an Oregon policy or carrier. Get quotes. Rates often change with a new state. |
| Renters / homeowners insurance | **J** | 2–3 weeks before move. Cancel old, start new policy effective on your Oregon move-in date. | Don't have a gap — overlap by one day if anything. |
| Health insurance | **J** | Within 30–60 days of the move (this is a qualifying life event). Notify your employer or marketplace. | Moving states triggers a Special Enrollment Period. Update your plan. |

## FINANCIAL

| Service | Who | When to Notify | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Banks and credit unions | **J** | 1–2 weeks before move. Update address online or by phone. | If your bank doesn't operate in Oregon, consider opening a new account before you close the old one. |
| Credit cards | **J** | 1–2 weeks before move. Update address online. | Fraud alerts sometimes trigger when cards are used in a new state. Give your card companies a heads-up. |
| Investment / retirement accounts | **J** | 1–2 weeks before move. | Update address and beneficiary info if needed. |
| Payroll / employer | **P** | 4 weeks before move. | Oregon income tax withholding needs to start. HR handles this, but flag it. |

## GOVERNMENT AND CIVIC

| Service | Who | When to Notify | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| USPS change of address | **J** | 2 weeks before move. File at usps.com. | Set the forwarding start date for 1–2 days before you leave Ohio. Lasts 12 months. |
| Ohio BMV | **M** | After Oregon registration is complete. | Cancel Ohio plates and registration. |
| Oregon DMV | **M** | Within the required window after establishing residency (verify current deadline). | License, registration, title transfer, emissions if applicable. |
| Voter registration | **J** | After you get your Oregon license. | Oregon has automatic voter registration through the DMV; verify at sos.oregon.gov. |
| IRS | **J** | On your next tax return. | Use your new address. No separate notification needed. |
| Social Security Administration | **J** | After the move. Update at ssa.gov or in person. | Important for mail delivery. |

| Service | Who | When | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gym membership | **P** | 2–4 weeks before move. Check cancellation terms — some require 30 days' written notice. | Some national chains allow a location transfer instead. |
| CSA / meal delivery / grocery delivery | **J** | 1–2 weeks before move. | Cancel or pause before the next billing cycle. |

# SUBSCRIPTIONS AND MEMBERSHIPS (continued)

| Service | Who | When | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gym membership | **P** | 2–4 weeks before move. Check cancellation terms — some require 30 days' written notice. | Some national chains allow a location transfer instead. |
| CSA / meal delivery / grocery delivery | **J** | 1–2 weeks before move. | Cancel or pause before the next billing cycle. |
| Newspaper / magazine subscriptions | **J** | 1–2 weeks before move. Update address online or cancel. | Some transfer automatically with USPS forwarding, but not reliably. |
| Amazon / online shopping defaults | **J** | Moving day or the day before. | Update default shipping address, payment method zip code, and Prime delivery preferences. |
| Library cards | **J** | Return all items 1 week before move. | Cancel or let it lapse. Sign up for an Oregon library card after arrival — many Oregon systems offer instant digital cards. |
| Pharmacy / prescription auto-refills | **M** | 2–3 weeks before move. Transfer prescriptions to an Oregon pharmacy or ask your doctor to send new scripts. | Fill a 90-day supply before you leave if your insurance allows it. |
| Pet services (groomer, walker, daycare, Chewy auto-ship) | **M** | 1–2 weeks before move. | Update Chewy or auto-ship addresses. Cancel local services. |
| House cleaner / lawn care / snow removal | **P** | 2–4 weeks before move. Give them proper notice. | You may want one final cleaning visit the day before the move. |
| Security system / alarm monitoring | **J** | 2–4 weeks before move. Check contract terms — some have early termination fees. | Return equipment or schedule a removal if it's leased. |
| Storage unit (if you have one) | **J** | 1–2 weeks before move. Clear it out and give written notice. | Most require 30 days' notice to avoid an extra month's billing. Check your agreement. |
| Dentist / doctor / therapist | **J** | 2–4 weeks before move. Request copies of records. | Most offices need a signed release form. Ask for digital copies if available. |
| Veterinarian (Ohio) | **M** | 1–2 weeks before move. Request full records if you haven't already. | Confirm they'll send records to your new Oregon vet. |
| Religious organization / club memberships | **J** | 1–2 weeks before move. | Notify as a courtesy and update any tithing or auto-pay. |
| Childcare / school (if applicable) | n/a | n/a | Not applicable for your household, but listed for completeness. |

---

## HOW TO TRACK CANCELLATIONS

Create a simple spreadsheet or note with four columns: **Service Name, Date Notified, Confirmation Number, Final Bill Date.** Check each one off as you get written confirmation. Screenshot every cancellation confirmation email or chat transcript. Services that don't confirm in writing should be followed up with a phone call.

---
---

# COPY-PASTE TEMPLATES

Each template below is meant to be edited with your real details. Brackets [ ] mark the parts you fill in. Keep the tone short and professional — these aren't negotiation letters, they're notifications.

---

## 1. LANDLORD NOTICE — Written Notice to Vacate

**Who sends:** J (both names on the lease should sign or be named)
**How to send:** Email and printed letter if your lease requires written notice. Send both to be safe. Keep a copy.
**When to send:** Check your lease for the required notice period (usually 30 or 60 days). Send on or before that deadline.

**Subject line:** Notice to Vacate — [Your Address] — Effective [Date]

```
Dear [Landlord Name / Property Management Company],

This letter serves as our formal [30/60]-day notice to vacate the property at [full address, including unit number]. Our intended move-out date is [date]. We request a move-out inspection and ask that our security deposit be returned to our forwarding address: [new Oregon address or a reliable forwarding address].

Please let us know if you need anything else from us to complete the move-out process.

Sincerely,
[Your Name] and [Partner's Name]
[Phone number]
[Email]
```

---

## 2. CABLE / INTERNET — Cancellation Request

**Who sends:** P
**How to send:** Phone is fastest, but follow up with email or chat so you have a written record. Ask for a confirmation number.
**When to send:** 1–2 weeks before move-out date.

**Subject line:** Account Cancellation Request — Account #[number] — Effective [Date]

```
Hello,

I'd like to cancel our internet/cable service at [full address] effective [last day of service, ideally the day after you move out]. Our account number is [number] under the name [name on the account].

Please confirm the cancellation, the final bill amount, and instructions for returning any equipment (modem, router, cable box). I'd like written confirmation of this cancellation by email.

Thank you,
[Name]
[Phone number]
```

---

## 3. ELECTRICITY / GAS — Stop Service

**Who sends:** M
**How to send:** Most utilities let you do this online or by phone. Follow up with email if possible.
**When to send:** 5–7 business days before move-out.

**Subject line:** Request to Disconnect Service — Account #[number] — [Address]

```
Hello,

Please schedule a final meter read and disconnect service at [full address] effective [date, the day after move-out]. Our account number is [number] under [name on the account].

Please send the final bill to our new address: [Oregon address]. If a deposit refund is due, please send it to the same address.

Thank you,
[Name]
[Phone number]
```

*Note: Send a nearly identical message to start service in Oregon, replacing "disconnect" with "start new service" and including your requested start date, the Oregon address, and your SSN or ID if the provider requires it for a new account.*

---

## 4. WATER / SEWER / TRASH — Stop Service

**Who sends:** P
**How to send:** Phone or the city's online portal. Many municipalities bundle these services.
**When to send:** 3–7 business days before move-out.

**Subject line:** Request to Close Water/Sewer/Trash Account — [Address]

```
Hello,

We are moving out of [full address] on [date] and would like to close our water, sewer, and trash service effective that date. Our account number is [number, if you have one] under [name].

Please send the final bill to: [Oregon address]. Let us know if a final meter read is required or if we need to do anything else on our end.

Thank you,
[Name]
[Phone number]
```

---

## 5. USPS CHANGE OF ADDRESS

**Who sends:** J (each person files individually if you have different last names; file together if you share a last name and want all household mail forwarded)

**When to send:** 2 weeks before move-out. Set the forwarding start date for 1–2 days before you leave Ohio.

*There's no email template needed for this one — the USPS online form walks you through it. Here's what you'll need to have ready:*

```
Information to have on hand:
- Full legal name(s)
- Current Ohio address (the one you're leaving)
- New Oregon address (the one you're moving to)
- Start date for forwarding (set this 1–2 days before move-out)
- Email address (for confirmation)
- Credit or debit card (for the $1.10 identity verification fee)
- Whether this is for an individual, family, or business
```

*After you submit, USPS sends a confirmation email and a physical validation letter to your old address within 5 business days. If you don't receive the validation letter, call 1-800-ASK-USPS to confirm the request went through. Mail forwarding lasts 12 months for first-class mail. Packages and periodicals forward for shorter periods. Don't rely on forwarding as a long-term solution — update your address directly with every sender that matters.*

# OHIO → OREGON DRIVE ROUTE PLANNER

**Route:** I-80 West across Ohio, Indiana, Iowa, Nebraska, Wyoming → I-84 West through Idaho and into Oregon. This is roughly 2,300–2,500 miles depending on your starting city in Ohio and destination in Oregon. The I-80/I-84 corridor is the most common and well-serviced route for this move.

**Important caveat:** Drive times below assume decent weather and no major construction. Check road conditions before each day's departure, especially through Wyoming and the Blue Mountains in Oregon. In late fall or winter, carry chains and check WYDOT and TripCheck.com (Oregon) for pass conditions. Summer is generally clear but can be very hot through Nebraska and Wyoming.

---

## 3-DAY OPTION (long days, not ideal with a dog)

| Day | Start → End | Miles | Drive Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ohio → Lincoln/Omaha, NE | ~750–800 | ~11–12 hrs | Very long. Only do this if you leave at dawn. |
| 2 | Lincoln/Omaha → Salt Lake City, UT | ~850 | ~12–13 hrs | Brutal. Wyoming is beautiful but empty. |
| 3 | Salt Lake City → Oregon destination | ~600–750 | ~9–11 hrs | Through Boise and into Oregon on I-84. |

This pace is hard on you and harder on the dog. Not recommended unless you're under a strict deadline.

---

## 4-DAY OPTION (recommended with a dog)

This is the pace I'd suggest. Days are manageable, the dog gets real breaks, and you arrive without being wrecked.

**Day 1: Ohio → Des Moines or Omaha area**
- Miles: ~550–650 depending on where in Ohio you start
- Drive time: ~8–9 hours with stops
- Terrain: flat, easy, Interstate the whole way
- Dog stops: rest areas every 60–90 miles along I-80 through Indiana and Iowa are plentiful and usually have grass
- Overnight: Des Moines or Omaha. Both have plenty of dog-friendly hotels and restaurants with patios.

**Day 2: Des Moines/Omaha → Cheyenne or Rawlins, WY**
- Miles: ~500–550
- Drive time: ~7–8 hours with stops
- Terrain: Nebraska is flat and long. Western Nebraska gets more scenic. Wyoming starts climbing.
- Dog stops: rest areas thin out in western Nebraska. Plan fuel and bathroom stops at exits with truck stops. Bring water for the dog at every stop.
- Overnight: Cheyenne is a bigger town with more hotel options. Rawlins is smaller but puts you further west and shortens Day 3. Either works.

**Day 3: Cheyenne/Rawlins → Boise, ID**
- Miles: ~550–650
- Drive time: ~8–10 hours with stops
- Terrain: across Wyoming on I-80, then north on US-30 or I-15 through Pocatello to I-84 near Twin Falls, then west to Boise. Alternatively, continue I-80 to I-84 through Ogden/Salt Lake City if you prefer that junction. The SLC route adds ~30 min but is better-serviced.
- Dog stops: Wyoming has long empty stretches. Fill up on gas whenever you're below half a tank. Rest areas exist but are spaced out. Idaho is better.
- Overnight: Boise. Good city with dog-friendly parks, restaurants, and hotels. The Boise River Greenbelt is a great place to let the dog stretch.

**Day 4: Boise → Oregon destination**
- Miles: ~350–450 to Portland metro, ~250–350 to Bend area, ~400–500 to Eugene area
- Drive time: ~5–8 hours depending on destination
- Terrain: I-84 follows the Snake River, then climbs through the Blue Mountains near La Grande and Pendleton, then descends along the Columbia River Gorge into Portland. If your destination is south of Portland, you'll peel off onto US-97 or other routes.
- Dog stops: good rest areas along I-84. The Columbia Gorge is stunning — if you have time, stop at a viewpoint.
- Arrival: aim to arrive by mid-afternoon so you have daylight to unload essentials and set up the dog's space.

---

## DOG TRAVEL TIPS FOR THE DRIVE

Stop every 2–3 hours for 15–20 minutes. Let the dog walk, sniff, drink water, and go to the bathroom. Bring a gallon jug of water from home so the dog's stomach doesn't react to changing water sources along the route.

Never leave the dog in a parked car, even with windows cracked. Summer temps in Nebraska and Wyoming can push a parked car past 120°F in minutes.

Feed the dog a light meal in the morning and a normal meal at the hotel in the evening. Some dogs get carsick if they eat a full meal before driving. Keep treats small and infrequent.

A crate or crash-tested harness is safer than letting the dog roam the car. If the dog is anxious, a Thundershirt, calming chews, or a vet-prescribed mild sedative can help. Test any medication on a short drive before the trip so you know how the dog reacts.

Bring a lint roller and a seat cover. You'll thank yourself.

---

## DOG-FRIENDLY HOTEL CHAINS AND TYPICAL PET FEES

Call ahead or check the specific location's pet policy before booking. Policies vary by franchise location even within the same chain. Fees listed are typical ranges as of 2024–2025 and may have changed.

| Chain | Typical Pet Fee | Weight Limit | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| La Quinta by Wyndham | Usually free, no fee | Generally no weight limit | One of the most consistently dog-friendly chains. No deposit at most locations. Two pets max at most locations. |
| Motel 6 / Studio 6 | Usually free, no fee | Generally no weight limit | Budget option. Quality varies. Call ahead to confirm. |
| Red Roof Inn | Usually free, no fee | Generally no weight limit (one pet) | Similar to Motel 6 in price and variability. |
| Best Western | $10–$50/night per pet | Varies by location, often 80 lbs | Some locations don't accept pets. Always call. |
| Holiday Inn / IHG brands | $25–$75/night or per stay | Varies, often 50–80 lbs | Pet fees and weight limits vary significantly by location. |
| Drury Inn & Suites | $35–$50/night per room | Usually 80 lbs | Includes free hot breakfast, which helps the budget. |
| Marriott (select brands) | $25–$150 per stay or per night | Varies widely by brand and location | Residence Inn and TownePlace Suites tend to be more pet-friendly than full-service Marriotts. |
| Kimpton Hotels | Usually no fee | No weight limit | Upscale option, not everywhere along I-80. |

**Booking tip:** BringFido.com lets you filter by pet-friendly hotels along a route. Book refundable rates when possible since your driving pace might change.

---

## EMERGENCY VET CLINICS ALONG THE ROUTE

**Important:** Verify hours, availability, and addresses before you travel. Emergency vet clinics change ownership, hours, and locations. Save these as contacts in your phone before you leave, and do a quick Google Maps search the morning of each driving day to confirm the nearest 24-hour option along that day's stretch.

**Salt Lake City area (Day 2 or 3, depending on route)**
- Search for "24 hour emergency vet Salt Lake City" the morning you'll be in that area
- The SLC metro area generally has multiple 24-hour emergency veterinary hospitals. Look near I-15 and I-80 interchange area for quick highway access.
- There are also emergency vet options in Ogden (north of SLC) and Provo (south) if you're passing through those areas instead.

**Boise, ID (Day 3 overnight)**
- Search for "24 hour emergency vet Boise Idaho" before you arrive
- Boise is a mid-size metro and typically has at least one or two 24-hour emergency vet hospitals. Your hotel front desk can also help in a pinch.
- If you're stopping in Twin Falls earlier in the day, search for emergency vet options there as well, though options are more limited in smaller Idaho cities.

**Pendleton / La Grande, OR (Day 4, mid-route)**
- These are small towns. 24-hour emergency vet availability is limited and may not exist locally.
- Search for "emergency vet Pendleton Oregon" and "emergency vet La Grande Oregon" before entering this stretch. Identify the nearest option and save the number.
- If this stretch concerns you, consider stopping in La Grande for a break and assessing the dog's condition. The next well-serviced area is the Tri-Cities in Washington (Kennewick/Richland, about 45 minutes north of I-84 via US-395) or The Dalles and Hood River further west along I-84.
- Once you reach the Portland metro area, multiple 24-hour emergency veterinary hospitals are available.

**General advice for emergencies on the road:** Keep your dog's medical records, medications, and your home vet's phone number accessible. If the dog has a known condition (seizures, allergies, heart issues), write a one-page medical summary with the dog's name, breed, weight, conditions, medications, and your vet's contact info. Keep it in the dog travel kit. Any emergency vet will appreciate having that information immediately.

# FIRST-WEEK UNPACK PRIORITY CHECKLIST

Don't try to unpack everything in the first week. Unpack what you need to function, sleep, eat, and work. Everything else can wait.

---

**BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE (arrival day, first 30 minutes)**

- [ ] Walk through every room and photograph existing damage before anything is unloaded
- [ ] Confirm water, electricity, gas, and heat/AC are working
- [ ] Locate the breaker box, water shutoff valve, and gas shutoff
- [ ] Set up the dog's space first: water bowl, food bowl, bed or blanket, one toy, in a quiet room away from the chaos. Close the door or use a baby gate so the dog has a safe retreat.
- [ ] Unload your personal overnight bags and the moving day car kit

**DAY 1 EVENING — sleep and basic function**

- [ ] Set up beds or air mattresses. Put on sheets and pillows. This is the single most important unpack task — a bad first night makes everything harder.
- [ ] Unpack the bathroom OPEN FIRST box: toilet paper, towels, soap, toothbrushes, shower curtain
- [ ] Unpack the kitchen OPEN FIRST box: coffee maker, mugs, one pot, one pan, dish soap, sponge, paper towels, trash bags
- [ ] Set up one lamp or light source in each room you'll use tonight
- [ ] Plug in and charge all phones and laptops
- [ ] Take the dog for a walk around the neighborhood. Let them sniff and start learning the new territory.
- [ ] Order food or eat something simple. You are not cooking tonight.

**DAY 2 — kitchen and living room basics**

- [ ] Unpack remaining kitchen boxes marked OPEN FIRST and SOON
- [ ] Put away dishes, utensils, pots, and pans. Don't worry about optimizing cabinet layout yet.
- [ ] Set up the coffee station properly. Morale matters.
- [ ] Unpack the living room seating area: couch, chairs, TV if you want it. You need a place to sit and decompress.
- [ ] Break down empty boxes as you go and stack them in the garage or a closet. They pile up fast.

**DAY 3 — bedrooms and closets**

- [ ] Unpack clothing into closets and dressers. Hang what you can; stack the rest.
- [ ] Set up nightstands, lamps, alarm clocks
- [ ] Make the bed properly — this is now home, not a campsite
- [ ] Unpack the linen closet: towels, sheets, blankets

**DAY 4 — home office and connectivity**

- [ ] Confirm internet is installed and working. If not, troubleshoot or call the provider.
- [ ] Set up your desk, monitor, keyboard, and chair
- [ ] Test your work setup: VPN, video calls, printer if needed
- [ ] Unpack office supplies and files

**DAY 5 — bathrooms, remaining kitchen, and dog admin**

- [ ] Fully unpack all bathrooms
- [ ] Unpack remaining kitchen boxes (the LATER ones — bakeware, specialty appliances, entertaining supplies)
- [ ] Call the Oregon vet to confirm the first appointment
- [ ] Walk to or drive by the nearest grocery store, pharmacy, and gas station. Learn the neighborhood basics.
- [ ] Update the dog's microchip with the new address

**DAYS 6–7 — garage, storage, decor, and settling in**

- [ ] Unpack garage and storage boxes. Set up tools, cleaning supplies, outdoor gear.
- [ ] Hang pictures and artwork. This is when a place starts feeling like home.
- [ ] Unpack remaining decor, books, and personal items
- [ ] Do a full grocery shop for the week ahead
- [ ] Take the dog to explore a local park or trail
- [ ] Sit down together and make a list of anything you still need to buy, fix, or handle in week two

**WEEK 2 AND BEYOND**

- [ ] Oregon DMV: driver's license and vehicle registration
- [ ] Oregon dog license from your county or city
- [ ] Emissions test if required
- [ ] Find a dentist, doctor, and pharmacy
- [ ] Update remaining subscriptions and memberships with new address
- [ ] Explore your neighborhood for real. Find the coffee shop, the hardware store, the good takeout place, the dog-friendly spots.

## SPREADSHEET TIPS

**Column-by-column guidance:**

"Box ID" uses the room abbreviation scheme above (KIT-01, BED1-03, etc.). Keep it consistent.

"Box # / Total" is the count within that room. You won't know the total until you're done packing that room, so leave the total blank and fill it in at the end. Write it on the labels at the same time.

"Contents (short)" is what goes on the physical label — a quick 3–5 word description you can read from across the room.

"Contents (detailed)" is the full list of what's inside. This is what you'll search when you're in Oregon wondering which box has the can opener.

"Est. Weight" helps movers and helps you decide what goes on the truck first (heavy on the bottom). Don't overthink it. "Light," "medium," and "heavy" work too if you don't want to guess pounds.

"Fragile" matches the checkbox on the label.

"Priority" matches the label: OPEN FIRST, SOON, or LATER.

"Destination" is where the box goes in the new home. This matches the "Destination" line on the label and aligns with the furniture placement worksheets you're taping to each door.

"Mover Notes" is anything special: "keep upright," "do not stack," "unload last," "this box is weirdly heavy."

"Packed By" is M, P, or J. Useful when one of you is looking for something and the other one packed it.

"Packed Date" and "Opened Date" help you track progress and notice if any box never got opened, which probably means you didn't need what was inside.

"Photo" is optional but useful. Snap a photo of the box contents before you seal it, name the file to match the Box ID, and save to a shared folder (Google Photos album or Google Drive folder). If you file a claim for damage, you'll have photographic proof of condition and contents.

---

## SHARING THE SPREADSHEET

Create the sheet in Google Sheets and share it with your partner so both of you can update it in real time from your phones. Bookmark it on both phones. As you pack each box, one person fills in the row while the other tapes the label. It takes about 60 seconds per box once you're in a rhythm.
